opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started somewhat by accident, but it's become the work I care about most. Early in my career I was doing computational work in imaging, and I ended up collaborating with surgeons and radiologists who treated patients with liver and pancreatic tumors. Once you sit in those clinics and see what these patients face, it's hard to walk away.

Pancreatic cancer in particular has one of the worst survival rates of any cancer. Most patients are diagnosed late, when surgery is no longer an option, and even for those who can have surgery, recurrence is common. Liver cancers, both primary tumors and metastases that spread there from places like the colon, have similar challenges. In many cases we don't have good ways to predict who will respond to which treatment, or who is at highest risk of the disease coming back.

From a machine learning perspective, that's where I think we can make a real difference. These patients get a lot of imaging, CT scans especially, and there's information in those images that the human eye just can't pick up. Subtle texture patterns in the tissue, for example, might tell us something about the tumor's biology or how aggressive it's likely to be. If we can extract that signal and turn it into something clinicians can act on, like deciding who should get more aggressive therapy or who should be monitored more closely, it could change outcomes for a group of patients who've had very few good options.

So it's partly the scientific challenge, and partly that the need is so great. When the outcomes are this poor, even incremental progress matters enormously to patients and their families.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that these are the cancers where the need is most acute and where I think computation can actually move the needle. Pancreatic cancer in particular has a five-year survival rate that has barely budged in decades. Liver cancers, both primary tumors and metastases that spread from the colon, are also extremely hard to treat, and a lot of the decision-making still comes down to a surgeon or radiologist looking at a scan and making a judgment call.

I came into this through surgery, actually. I spent years at Memorial Sloan Kettering working alongside surgeons in the hepatopancreatobiliary service, and what struck me was how much information is sitting in a routine CT scan that nobody is quantifying. We'd see two patients with tumors that looked almost identical on imaging, and one would respond beautifully to chemotherapy while the other wouldn't, or one would have a complication after surgery and the other wouldn't. The imaging had to be telling us something, we just weren't reading it in a way a human eye can pick up.

So the focus for me is on using machine learning to pull out those patterns: predicting who will respond to a given treatment, who is a good surgical candidate, how a tumor is likely to behave. For pancreas cancer, where many patients are diagnosed too late for surgery, even earlier detection or better triage could be a big deal. And these organs are also just technically interesting problems. The liver is a large, deformable organ with complex vasculature, and the pancreas is small, hard to see, and surrounded by structures that confuse segmentation algorithms. If you can make these methods work there, you learn a lot that transfers elsewhere.

But ultimately it comes back to the patients. I've sat in tumor boards and seen how little we have to offer some of these people, and I'd like to change that.
